title: Introduction to Prefix Sum
description: Understand how prefix sums store cumulative values to make repeated calculations faster

sections.title: 2. What is a prefix sum array?
3. How Prefix Sum Answers Range Queries

blocks.text: A preprocessing technique that turns repeated O(n) range queries into O(1) lookups one of the most widely used tricks in competitive programming and interviews.

blocks.caption: Prefix Sum Array Visualization — Array [2,4,1,7,3] with cumulative sums

blocks.text: Imagine you have an array and you're asked: "What is the sum of elements from index 2 to index 5?" Easy enough. But what if you're asked this question 10,000 times on the same array?
The naive approach recalculates the sum each time
O(n) per query, O(n × q) total.
For large arrays and many queries, this is too slow.
Prefix sum precomputes a helper array once in O(n), after which every range query is answered in O(1).
Trade-off: spend O(n) time and O(n) space once to build the prefix array. Every range sum query after that is a single subtraction O(1).

content.title: 2. What is a prefix sum array?

blocks.text: Given array arr, the prefix sum array prefix is defined so that prefix[i] stores the sum of all elements from index 0 up to and including index i.
prefix[i] = arr[0] + arr[1] + ... + arr[i]
For example, prefix[4] = 3+1+4+1+5 = 14. It's the running total as you scan left to right.
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
Understanding:

items: Step 1: Start with the first element. The first element is 3, so the first prefix sum is also 3.

blocks.text: Prefix: 3

items: Step 2: Move to the next element 1. Add it to the previous prefix sum (3 + 1 = 4).

blocks.text: Prefix: 3, 4

items: Step 3: Move to element 4. Add it to the previous prefix sum (4 + 4 = 8).

blocks.text: Prefix: 3, 4, 8

items: Step 4: Move to element 1. Add it to the previous prefix sum (8 + 1 = 9).

blocks.text: Prefix: 3, 4, 8, 9

items: Step 5: Move to element 5. Add it to the previous prefix sum (9 + 5 = 14).

blocks.text: Prefix: 3, 4, 8, 9, 14

items: Step 6: Move to element 9. Add it to the previous prefix sum (14 + 9 = 23).

blocks.text: Prefix: 3, 4, 8, 9, 14, 23

items: Step 7: Move to element 2. Add it to the previous prefix sum (23 + 2 = 25).

blocks.text: Prefix: 3, 4, 8, 9, 14, 23, 25

items: Step 8: Move to element 6. Add it to the previous prefix sum (25 + 6 = 31).

blocks.text: Final Prefix Array: 3, 4, 8, 9, 14, 23, 25, 31
Key Idea: Each prefix value stores the sum of all elements from index 0 up to that position. It is simply a running total as you move from left to right.

To find the sum of elements from index l to index r (inclusive), use:
Why does this work?prefix[r]contains the sum from 0 to r.prefix[l−1]contains the sum from 0 to l−1. Subtract them and the overlap cancels, leaving exactly the sum from l to r.

content.title: 3. How Prefix Sum Answers Range Queries

blocks.text: This diagram shows how a range sum query is answered using a prefix sum array.
We want to find the sum of elements from index 2 to 5 in the original array. These highlighted elements are 4, 1, 5, and 9. If we add them directly, the answer is:
4 + 1 + 5 + 9 = 19
Instead of adding all elements one by one every time, we use the prefix sum array. The value at prefix[5] = 23 tells us the sum of all elements from index 0 to 5:
However, this includes the elements before our range (3 and 1). To remove them, we subtract prefix[1] = 4, which represents the sum of elements from index 0 to 1:
3 + 1 = 4
After subtracting:
23 - 4 = 19
This leaves only the sum of elements from index 2 to 5, which is exactly the range we wanted.
The key idea is that prefix[r] contains the sum from index 0 to r. By subtracting prefix[l-1], we remove everything before index l and are left with only the required range.
That's why the range sum formula is:
sum(l, r) = prefix[r] - prefix[l - 1]
Using this trick, any range sum can be found in O(1) time instead of scanning the array every time.
Building the prefix array
The build step is a single left-to-right pass. Each cell equals the previous prefix value plus the current array element.
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">

Many competitive programmers use a 1-indexed prefix array of size n+1, where prefix[0] = 0. This eliminates the l == 0 edge case entirely the formula is always prefix[r] - prefix[l-1] with no special case.
How it works:

items: prefix[0] = 0 acts as a dummy value.
prefix[i] stores the sum of the first i elements.
To find the sum from index l to r (1-indexed), subtract the sum before l from the sum up to r.
No special handling is needed when l = 1 because prefix[0] is already 0.

blocks.text: Example:

items: prefix = [0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14]
Sum from l = 3 to r = 5
prefix[5] - prefix[2] = 14 - 4 = 10
Result: 4 + 1 + 5 = 10.

blocks.text: In interviews, using 1-indexed prefix is often cleaner. You never need to handlel == 0separately. Pick one convention and stick with it mixing both causes bugs.

blocks.text: Prefix sum is for static arrays. If elements are updated frequently, use a Fenwick Tree (BIT) or Segment Tree instead they support O(log n) updates and queries.
The same idea extends to 2D grids. prefix[i][j] stores the sum of all elements in the rectangle from (0,0) to (i,j). A submatrix sum query then uses inclusion-exclusion:

codes.python:
def build_2d_prefix(grid):
    m = len(grid)
    n = len(grid[0])

    P = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]  # 1-indexed

    for i in range(1, m + 1):
        for j in range(1, n + 1):
            P[i][j] = (grid[i - 1][j - 1]
                       + P[i - 1][j]
                       + P[i][j - 1]
                       - P[i - 1][j - 1])

    return P


# Query sum of rectangle (r1,c1) to (r2,c2) - 1-indexed
def query_2d(P, r1, c1, r2, c2):
    return (P[r2][c2]
            - P[r1 - 1][c2]
            - P[r2][c1 - 1]
            + P[r1 - 1][c1 - 1])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    grid = [
        [1, 2, 3],
        [4, 5, 6],
        [7, 8, 9],
    ]
    P = build_2d_prefix(grid)
    print(query_2d(P, 1, 1, 2, 2))

blocks.text: How it works:

items: P[i][j] stores the sum of all elements in the rectangle from (1,1) to (i,j).
While building P, we add the top area and left area, then subtract the overlapping top-left area once.
To get the sum of any rectangle (r1,c1) to (r2,c2), start with the entire area up to (r2,c2).
Remove the rows above r1 and the columns before c1.
Since the top-left region gets removed twice, add it back once.
Range Sum Query: Build the prefix sum array once, then any range sum can be answered instantly using the stored cumulative sums. This is the most common use of prefix sums.
Subarray with Target Sum: As you traverse the array, use prefix sums to determine whether a previous sum exists that would make the current subarray equal to the target value.
Number of Subarrays with Sum K: Track how many times each prefix sum has appeared. Whenever a matching prefix sum is found, it indicates one or more valid subarrays ending at the current position.
Pivot Index / Balance Point: Find an index where the sum of all elements on the left equals the sum of all elements on the right. Prefix sums allow both sides to be calculated efficiently.
Even/Odd Prefix Sums: If two prefix sums have the same parity (both even or both odd), the subarray between them has an even sum. This observation is useful in parity-related problems.
Prefix XOR: Similar to prefix sums, but uses the XOR operation instead of addition. It allows XOR values of any range to be computed efficiently.
Prefix Product: Instead of storing cumulative sums, store cumulative products. This can be used to answer product queries on ranges, though special care is needed when zeros are present.
2D Prefix Sum: Extends the prefix sum concept to matrices. After preprocessing, the sum of any rectangular region can be obtained in constant time.

Difference Array + Prefix Sum: Used when many range updates are required. Instead of updating every element individually, only boundary positions are updated, and a final prefix sum pass reconstructs the result.

Prefix Sum + HashMap: A powerful interview pattern where prefix sums are stored in a hashmap. It is commonly used to solve problems involving target sums, counting subarrays, longest valid subarrays, and divisibility conditions in O(n) time.

blocks.text: Many medium/hard problems combine prefix sum with a hashmap to count or find subarrays. The template is always the same:

codes.python:
class Solution:
    def subarray_sum(self, nums, k):
        seen = {0: 1}  # prefix sum 0 seen once

        count = 0
        prefix = 0

        for num in nums:
            prefix += num

            # subarrays ending here with sum k
            count += seen.get(prefix - k, 0)

            seen[prefix] = seen.get(prefix, 0) + 1

        return count


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sol = Solution()
    nums = [1, 1, 1]
    print(sol.subarray_sum(nums, 2))

blocks.text: How it Works
Step 1: Start with prefix = 0 and store that prefix sum 0 has been seen once. This represents the empty subarray before the array begins.
Step 2: Traverse the array and keep updating the running prefix sum.
Step 3: At each position, calculate prefix - k. If this value has been seen before, then there exists a subarray ending at the current index whose sum is exactly k.
Step 4: Add the number of times prefix - k has appeared to the answer.
Step 5: Record the current prefix sum in the hashmap so future elements can use it.
Step 6: Continue until the entire array is processed. The final count represents the number of subarrays whose sum equals k.
Key Idea: If two prefix sums differ by k, then the elements between them must sum to k. The hashmap helps us find those previous prefix sums in O(1) time.
Theseen = {0: 1}initialization is critical. It handles the case where the subarray starts from index 0. Forgetting this is the single most common bug in this pattern.

Off-by-one: forgetting the l == 0 check with 0-indexed prefix use 1-indexed to avoid this entirely.
Not initializing seen = {0: 1} in the hashmap pattern misses subarrays starting from index 0.
Modifying the original array instead of building a separate prefix array.
Using prefix sum when the array has updates it requires O(n) rebuild. Use a Fenwick Tree instead.
In 2D prefix sum: getting the inclusion-exclusion formula wrong draw the rectangles and derive it from scratch if unsure.
Integer overflow: for large arrays with large values, use long long in C++.
